screens.title: On‑premise, Cloud, and Hybrid: tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a deployment model is one of the earliest production decisions and it shapes cost, control, and compliance. On‑premise deployments give you full control over hardware, networking, and data residency, which is often needed for strict regulatory environments. The tradeoff is higher capital expenditure and responsibility for patching, physical security, and capacity planning. Public cloud simplifies provisioning and scaling through managed services and elastic resources, but it adds considerations around vendor lock‑in, network egress costs, and the need to configure cloud network security correctly. Hybrid models try to combine the best of both worlds, placing sensitive data on-premise while leveraging cloud elasticity for peak loads. In practice, evaluate data residency, compliance, operational expertise, and growth patterns when deciding. A concrete example: if your ledger stores personally identifiable records subject to local residency laws, an on‑premise or single‑region private cloud deployment will simplify compliance. A common misconception is that cloud equals insecure; security controls can be robust in cloud environments but must be explicitly configured. Conclude by mapping your top three compliance or operational constraints and let those guide the deployment model.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Deployment Model Comparison

On‑premise, Cloud, and Hybrid: tradeoffs

Compare the environments and choose based on compliance, scalability, and operational cost.

On‑premise
Control & compliance
  • Max control over data residency and physical security.
  • High upfront cost; full operational responsibility.
  • Good fit when strict regulatory requirements exist.
Cloud
Elasticity & managed services
  • Fast provisioning and scaling; pay-as-you-go.
  • Requires careful network and cost management.
  • Suitable when you need rapid scale and operator efficiency.
Hybrid
Selective distribution
  • Sensitive data on-prem, compute-burst in cloud.
  • Complex networking and identity integration.
  • Useful for phased migrations or mixed compliance demands.
Example

A financial firm keeps ledger nodes on premise for residency while using cloud for analytics nodes that read anonymized state for reporting.

Key Takeaway

Start with constraints. Let compliance and required control determine the model, then optimize for cost and scale.

screens.title: Designing for High Availability (HA)
screens.narratorSegment: High availability for Fabric means designing redundancy and failover for the components the network cannot run without. Orderer nodes, especially when using a Raft cluster, must be spread across failure domains and have stable, low‑latency network links to peers. Use at least three orderer nodes for quorum and consider load balancing for client connections. Peers should be deployed with redundancy per organization so endorsement and ledger replication survive node failures. For critical organizations, run multiple peers with separate storage to avoid a single-disk failure taking down state. Use replication for databases and fast storage for LevelDB when disk input and output is a bottleneck. A common pitfall is concentrating orderers or peers in one availability zone; that undermines HA. Also plan for graceful restart: ensure persistent volumes and configuration management keep peers consistent after restarts. Finally, implement health checks, readiness probes, and automated failover scripts or orchestration rules so your cluster detects and recovers from component failures quickly. Designing for High Availability (HA) means place orderers and peers across separate failure zones, use quorum for ordering, and ensure storage redundancy to maintain ledger availability.. In practical terms, redundancy and failover for orderers and peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › High Availability

Designing for High Availability (HA)

Ensure ordering and endorsement survive failures through redundancy and orchestration.

Orderer HA
  • Run a Raft cluster with an odd number of nodes (three or five) across failure domains.
  • Provide stable low-latency network links and persistent storage for orderer logs.
  • Use load balancers for client connections and plan for leader election behavior.
Common mistake: co-locating all orderers in the same zone.
Peer HA
  • Deploy multiple peers per organization with replicated state to withstand node loss.
  • Choose storage that matches LevelDB or CouchDB needs; use fast disks for high I/O.
  • Automate health checks and readiness probes to trigger failover or replacement.
Pro tip: test failover by simulating zone failure and observing endorsement and commit behavior.
Key Takeaway

Design for distributed failure domains, persistent storage, and automated recovery to keep ordering and endorsement available under realistic failures.

screens.title: TLS, Certificates, and Fabric CAs
screens.narratorSegment: Transport Layer Security is the backbone of secure communication in Fabric. Every component — peers, orderers, chaincode containers, and client SDKs — should use TLS to prevent eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. Fabric uses certificates issued by Certificate Authorities; these certificates authenticate identities and enable policy enforcement. Managing certificate lifecycles is a continuous operational task: implement rotation schedules, revoke compromised certificates, and audit CA configurations. A misconception is that TLS is a one-and-done setting; in production, you must monitor certificate expiry and automate rotations to avoid unexpected service outages. Also document trust anchors and ensure all systems accept the same CA roots. A concrete example: schedule certificate rotation for a CA that issues peer identities every six months, automate distribution of new certificates to pods or servers, and run a staged rollout to prevent simultaneous expiration. Finally, pair TLS with network segmentation and firewall rules so only required ports are exposed between components. TLS, Certificates, and Fabric CAs means tls plus disciplined ca lifecycle management prevents outages and maintains trust across fabric components.. In practical terms, why tls and certificate lifecycle matter for fabric communication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Security Fundamentals

TLS, Certificates, and Fabric CAs

Secure all internal and external communications and manage certificate lifecycles proactively.

TLS for all channels

Enforce TLS between peers, orderers, CAs, and client SDKs to protect data in transit and authenticate endpoints.

Certificate lifecycle

Automate issuance, rotation, and revocation. Monitor expirations and stage rollouts to avoid service interruptions.

Fabric CA operations

Secure CA hosts, back up CA keys, and restrict CA access. Treat CA infrastructure as highly sensitive and auditable.

Example

Rotate CA-issued peer certificates on a schedule and perform a staged rollout: test on a single org, then update remaining peers to avoid simultaneous expiration.

Common mistake

Relying on manual certificate updates. Manual rotations lead to missed expiries and outages in production.

screens.title: Hardware Security Modules and key protection
screens.narratorSegment: Hardware Security Modules provide a tamper-resistant environment for key generation and cryptographic operations. In production, you should evaluate HSMs for protecting private keys of orderers, CAs, and high‑privilege identities. An HSM never exposes private keys in plain storage; it performs sign and decrypt operations inside secure hardware. This reduces the blast radius if a host is compromised. When designing HSM integration, decide whether to use network-attached HSMs or cloud HSM services, and plan for connectivity, latency, and failover for the HSM cluster. Backups of key material differ: you store encrypted key backups or leverage HSM key replication features rather than exporting raw keys. A common misconception is that HSMs remove the need for other security measures; they do not. Continue to apply OS hardening, access controls, and network segmentation around HSM hosts. Finally, ensure your deployment automates key provisioning to prevent manual errors and to document KMS usage for audits. Hardware Security Modules and key protection means use hsms for high‑value private keys to perform cryptographic ops in hardware and limit key export and exposure.. In practical terms, how hsms change key storage and cryptographic workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Key Management

Hardware Security Modules and key protection

HSMs provide tamper-resistant key storage and on‑device cryptographic operations — use them for critical Fabric identities.

What an HSM does

Generates keys inside secure hardware, performs signing/decryption inside device, and prevents key export in cleartext.

Operational considerations

Plan connectivity, latency, redundancy, and whether to use on-prem HSMs or cloud KMS offerings with HSM guarantees.

Backup & recovery

Use HSM replication or secure wrapped backups; treat key recovery as a high-risk operation that requires multi-person authorization.

Example

Store orderer and CA signing keys in an HSM and configure Fabric components to call the HSM for signing operations rather than reading keys from disk.

Misconception

An HSM is not a replacement for OS hardening and access controls; it complements a layered security posture.

screens.title: LevelDB vs CouchDB and resource sizing
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric supports different state database backends and the choice influences resource allocation. LevelDB is an embedded key-value store that typically requires less memory but benefits from strong disk input and output performance because its operations are disk-centric. CouchDB provides rich query capabilities and stores JSON documents; it can be more C P U and memory intensive when handling complex queries or large documents. When sizing peers, consider the interaction between chaincode complexity and the chosen state database. For example, if your chaincode performs many complex rich queries, CouchDB may simplify query logic but will require more R A M and C P U than LevelDB. Orderer sizing is influenced more by transaction throughput and consensus algorithm: Raft orderers need stable C P U and network to handle leader election and log replication. The practical approach is to prototype with expected workloads, measure C P U, R A M, and disk input and output, and then add headroom for peaks. Avoid underestimating disk input and output; slow disks are one of the most frequent causes of latency in peer commits. LevelDB vs CouchDB and resource sizing means choose leveldb for simple key lookups and couchdb for complex json queries, and size hardware according to those access patterns.. In practical terms, how database choice impacts cpu, memory, and disk requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › State Database & Sizing

LevelDB vs CouchDB and resource sizing

Database choice affects CPU, RAM, and disk I/O and should align with query patterns.

LevelDB
  • Embedded key-value store, efficient for simple gets and puts.
  • Typically lower RAM needs, but requires fast disk I/O.
  • Good when chaincode avoids complex JSON queries.
CouchDB
  • Supports rich JSON queries and complex views.
  • Higher RAM and CPU consumption under heavy query loads.
  • Prefer when chaincode requires frequent ad hoc queries over JSON state.
Sizing advice

Prototype against expected workloads, measure CPU, RAM, and disk I/O, and provide headroom. Fast SSDs often yield larger performance gains than adding CPU alone.

screens.title: Load Testing and Bottleneck Identification
screens.narratorSegment: Load testing validates your sizing assumptions and uncovers bottlenecks before production. Start by creating realistic transaction profiles that mirror expected client behavior: endorsement patterns, transaction sizes, and rate. Use synthetic load generators to replay those profiles while you collect metrics for C P U, memory, disk input and output, network latency, ordering throughput, and commit latency. Focus tests on chaincode execution and ordering paths separately to isolate bottlenecks. For example, run a chaincode-heavy workload on peers with CouchDB and observe C P U and R A M; then run a high-throughput, small-transaction mix to observe orderer performance and network saturation. Analyze metrics to answer: is C P U pegged, is disk input and output the limiting factor, or is network bandwidth causing latency? A common misinterpretation is to only look at average latency — also inspect percentiles and tail latency which often reveal real user impact. Finally, plan scale strategies: vertical scaling when a single component is resource-bound, horizontal scaling when you can distribute load across more peers or orderers. Load Testing and Bottleneck Identification means use realistic load tests to reveal whether cpu, memory, disk i/o, or network are the real bottlenecks and then apply targeted scaling.. In practical terms, simulate realistic workloads and find where to scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Load Testing

Load Testing and Bottleneck Identification

Design tests that reflect production traffic, collect metrics, and examine percentiles to find real user impact.

Testing steps
  1. Define realistic transaction profiles and endorsement flows.
  2. Run separate tests for chaincode CPU and orderer throughput.
  3. Collect CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network, and latency percentiles.
Interpretation
  • High disk I/O suggests faster storage or sharding.
  • High CPU on peers suggests optimizing chaincode or adding replicas.
  • Network saturation calls for improved bandwidth or regional placement.
Example

Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Terminal Demo

Inspecting System Resources on Linux

Run these commands during load tests to understand host constraints that affect Fabric performance.

Command: top
top -b -n 1

Shows real-time CPU and per-process usage; use it to spot chaincode processes using excessive CPU during tests.

Command: free
free -h

Displays memory and swap usage in human-readable units; check for swap activity that signals insufficient RAM.

Command: iostat
iostat -xz 1 3

Reports disk throughput and average queue times. High await or %util suggests storage is the bottleneck.

Example workflow

While running a synthetic transaction load, capture top, free, and iostat outputs and correlate spikes with commit latency to determine whether to increase CPU, RAM, or switch to faster disks.

screens.title: Backup and Disaster Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: A robust backup and disaster recovery plan is required for business continuity. Back up ledger data, state databases, and cryptographic materials on a schedule that reflects your recovery point objectives. Ledger backups should be consistent and stored off-site or in an immutable store to protect against corruption or ransomware. For state databases like CouchDB, ensure consistency across replicas and include snapshots as part of your backup routine. Cryptographic material needs special handling: private keys must be backed up in encrypted form or managed through HSM replication; access to backup keys should be tightly controlled and audited. Regularly test restores in an isolated environment to validate procedures and recovery time objectives. A common mistake is only backing up data and not documenting the restore steps; a tested runbook speeds recovery and ensures you can bring the network back with correct identities and ordering state. Schedule periodic DR drills and update processes based on lessons learned. fullNarratorScript:
Moving a Hyperledger Fabric network into production means shifting from a developer sandbox to an operational system that must be secure, resilient, and measurable. In this lesson you'll learn how to assess infrastructure needs, choose between on-premise, cloud, or hybrid deployments, and apply a security-first approach to certificates and private keys. We'll explain why hardware sizing, reliable ordering and peer placement, and proper monitoring are not optional. You will see how Hardware Security Modules reduce risk for critical identities, why TLS and encrypted storage matter for every component, and how to formalize backups and disaster recovery. A practical checklist organizes these decisions into infrastructure, security, monitoring, backup, automation, and compliance. By the end you will be able to draft a production readiness checklist tailored to your organization and identify the first three operational steps to implement. Consider now which compliance or control requirement in your organization will most affect your deployment model.

In these objectives we focus on the practical skills that let you make deployment decisions and secure a Fabric network. First, you will learn to identify the infrastructure requirements for production: understand redundancy, network topology, and the tradeoffs between cloud, on‑premise, and hybrid deployments. Second, you will develop a security checklist that covers OS hardening, TLS configuration, certificate lifecycle, and key protection — enough to guide an implementation and audits. Third, you will be able to size your components by relating expected transaction throughput and chaincode complexity to C P U, R A M, disk input and output, and network bandwidth. Finally, you will learn secure strategies for managing cryptographic materials, including when to adopt a Hardware Security Module and how to back up keys securely. Each objective pairs a practical task with the reason it matters in production, so you can prioritize actions that reduce downtime, protect sensitive keys, and maintain compliance under real operational conditions.

Now we'll translate objectives into observable tasks you can perform and verify. For infrastructure, draft a topology diagram showing peer and orderer placement, subnets, and load balancers, and record failover points. For security, produce a documented checklist that lists TLS enforcement, CA certificate rotation, OS hardening steps, and HSM usage where applicable. For sizing, run an initial load test and map C P U, R A M, and disk input and output under baseline and peak scenarios; use these results to set resource margins rather than guessing. For cryptographic materials, create a key lifecycle plan that includes HSM integration or encrypted vaults, regular backups, and a recovery procedure. Each objective has an associated verification step: a topology diagram and load baseline, a signed audit checklist, a performance report showing threshold results, and a tested key restoration runbook. These concrete artifacts make the objectives auditable and actionable during a production readiness review.

Choosing a deployment model is one of the earliest production decisions and it shapes cost, control, and compliance. On‑premise deployments give you full control over hardware, networking, and data residency, which is often needed for strict regulatory environments. The tradeoff is higher capital expenditure and responsibility for patching, physical security, and capacity planning. Public cloud simplifies provisioning and scaling through managed services and elastic resources, but it adds considerations around vendor lock‑in, network egress costs, and the need to configure cloud network security correctly. Hybrid models try to combine the best of both worlds, placing sensitive data on-premise while leveraging cloud elasticity for peak loads. In practice, evaluate data residency, compliance, operational expertise, and growth patterns when deciding. A concrete example: if your ledger stores personally identifiable records subject to local residency laws, an on‑premise or single‑region private cloud deployment will simplify compliance. A common misconception is that cloud equals insecure; security controls can be robust in cloud environments but must be explicitly configured. Conclude by mapping your top three compliance or operational constraints and let those guide the deployment model.

High availability for Fabric means designing redundancy and failover for the components the network cannot run without. Orderer nodes, especially when using a Raft cluster, must be spread across failure domains and have stable, low‑latency network links to peers. Use at least three orderer nodes for quorum and consider load balancing for client connections. Peers should be deployed with redundancy per organization so endorsement and ledger replication survive node failures. For critical organizations, run multiple peers with separate storage to avoid a single-disk failure taking down state. Use replication for databases and fast storage for LevelDB when disk input and output is a bottleneck. A common pitfall is concentrating orderers or peers in one availability zone; that undermines HA. Also plan for graceful restart: ensure persistent volumes and configuration management keep peers consistent after restarts. Finally, implement health checks, readiness probes, and automated failover scripts or orchestration rules so your cluster detects and recovers from component failures quickly. Designing for High Availability (HA) means place orderers and peers across separate failure zones, use quorum for ordering, and ensure storage redundancy to maintain ledger availability.. In practical terms, redundancy and failover for orderers and peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transport Layer Security is the backbone of secure communication in Fabric. Every component — peers, orderers, chaincode containers, and client SDKs — should use TLS to prevent eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. Fabric uses certificates issued by Certificate Authorities; these certificates authenticate identities and enable policy enforcement. Managing certificate lifecycles is a continuous operational task: implement rotation schedules, revoke compromised certificates, and audit CA configurations. A misconception is that TLS is a one-and-done setting; in production, you must monitor certificate expiry and automate rotations to avoid unexpected service outages. Also document trust anchors and ensure all systems accept the same CA roots. A concrete example: schedule certificate rotation for a CA that issues peer identities every six months, automate distribution of new certificates to pods or servers, and run a staged rollout to prevent simultaneous expiration. Finally, pair TLS with network segmentation and firewall rules so only required ports are exposed between components. TLS, Certificates, and Fabric CAs means tls plus disciplined ca lifecycle management prevents outages and maintains trust across fabric components.. In practical terms, why tls and certificate lifecycle matter for fabric communication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hardware Security Modules provide a tamper-resistant environment for key generation and cryptographic operations. In production, you should evaluate HSMs for protecting private keys of orderers, CAs, and high‑privilege identities. An HSM never exposes private keys in plain storage; it performs sign and decrypt operations inside secure hardware. This reduces the blast radius if a host is compromised. When designing HSM integration, decide whether to use network-attached HSMs or cloud HSM services, and plan for connectivity, latency, and failover for the HSM cluster. Backups of key material differ: you store encrypted key backups or leverage HSM key replication features rather than exporting raw keys. A common misconception is that HSMs remove the need for other security measures; they do not. Continue to apply OS hardening, access controls, and network segmentation around HSM hosts. Finally, ensure your deployment automates key provisioning to prevent manual errors and to document KMS usage for audits. Fabric supports different state database backends and the choice influences resource allocation. LevelDB is an embedded key-value store that typically requires less memory but benefits from strong disk input and output performance because its operations are disk-centric. CouchDB provides rich query capabilities and stores JSON documents; it can be more C P U and memory intensive when handling complex queries or large documents. When sizing peers, consider the interaction between chaincode complexity and the chosen state database. For example, if your chaincode performs many complex rich queries, CouchDB may simplify query logic but will require more R A M and C P U than LevelDB. Orderer sizing is influenced more by transaction throughput and consensus algorithm: Raft orderers need stable C P U and network to handle leader election and log replication. The practical approach is to prototype with expected workloads, measure C P U, R A M, and disk input and output, and then add headroom for peaks. Avoid underestimating disk input and output; slow disks are one of the most frequent causes of latency in peer commits. Start by creating realistic transaction profiles that mirror expected client behavior: endorsement patterns, transaction sizes, and rate.
